title: Tobin's Wobbly Play
markdown:
In Willow Creek, where the river whispered secrets to the tall reeds and moonbeams spun silver threads through the trees, lived a mole named Tobin. Tobin wore spectacles that often tumbled down his twitching nose, and he had a heart that loved neatness more than anything. He was the stagehand for the Willow Creek Players, a very important job, especially for the annual village play.

Tobin loved his props. He polished each one until it shone like a dewdrop catching the sun. And his labels were the neatest, most sensible, most specific labels you ever did see.

The labels were so sensible. Oh, so sensible and neat.

For the king’s crown he wrote King’s Shiny Crown. For the knight’s sword, Brave Knight’s Sword. For a simple flowerpot, Pot for Plants. He believed that everyone, from the biggest badger to the smallest bug, should know exactly what a thing was for.

This year the play was The Princess and the Potting Shed. Aunt June the director, a badger with a voice like rustling leaves, had said, “Tobin, my dear, everything must be perfect. The play must go off without a hitch, like a ripe berry falling from a branch.” And Tobin had, of course, made it perfect. Or so he thought. He even tucked a tiny ladybug into a velvet pouch on the Princess’s costume, just in case she needed a friend.

The night of the play arrived with a soft hush that settled over Willow Creek like a mossy blanket. The audience — a chattering, rustling crowd of squirrels, sleepy hedgehogs, and even shy deer with wide curious eyes — settled into their mossy seats. Their noses twitched with happy anticipation. The curtains, woven from dandelion fluff and sparkling with starlight, parted with a whisper.

Iris the rabbit, playing the Princess, stepped forward. Her fur was the colour of toasted marshmallows, and her eyes sparkled like tiny blueberries. She was meant to pick up a rather lovely clay pot, which held a little sprout reaching for the light. But on the pot, Tobin had stuck a label that read Pot for Plants.

Iris blinked, her nose twitching. She looked at the label, then at the pot. “Oh my. I must attend to my Pot for Plants.” And with that she began to look very closely at the side of the pot, tapping it gently with a paw, as if she were a pottery expert finding a rare treasure.

The audience giggled, a sound like tiny bells. Aunt June, peeking from the wings, blinked. A tiny furrow appeared between her wise grey eyebrows.

Next, Bartholomew Bear, playing the Royal Gardener, lumbered on stage. He was a gentle giant, known for his booming laugh and his love of honey. He was supposed to hand Iris a watering can. But Tobin, with his love for clear labels, had labelled the watering can Watering Thingy.

Bartholomew hesitated, his big paws fumbling. “Ah, yes,” he rumbled, his voice deep as a stream, as he peered at the label. “I shall now present you with the Watering Thingy.” He gave it to her with a flourish that sent a puff of dust into the air. Iris, still looking at her pot, took it and poured a tiny dribble onto her own paw, as if testing it for watering plants.

The theatre filled with a ripple of chuckles, growing louder and warmer. Tobin, peeking from behind a painted cardboard tree that looked like a grumpy old oak, felt a peculiar twitch in his whiskers. His labels were so sensible. They were the most logical labels he had ever made. Why were they acting so odd? It was as if the labels had decided to take over the play.

A worry, like a late frost on a spring leaf, settled in Tobin’s chest. His need for order felt like a tangled knot in his tummy.

The Prince arrived, a dashing young fox with a very important speech about his love for the Princess. His speech was supposed to be, “My dearest Princess, your garden is a marvel.” But his cue card, placed next to a prop rose bush, had been labelled Pretty Flowers.

“My dearest Princess,” he stammered, his bushy tail giving a nervous flick as he read the label, “your Pretty Flowers are truly a marvel.” He then spent a long moment admiring the painted leaves, as if he had never seen a flower before in his whole life.

A wave of laughter, warm and rolling, swept through the audience. It was a joyous sound, like sunshine after a gentle rain. They were not just watching a play. They were watching words take a delightfully silly turn.

Tobin’s heart thumped like a trapped beetle against his ribs. He looked at his carefully arranged labels. This was not the perfect play he had imagined. It was a delightful, slightly wobbly, upside-down play. He imagined Aunt June’s frown growing even deeper.

He scurried backstage, his little mole legs a blur. He nearly tripped over a spare velvet curtain. Aunt June, though she usually enjoyed a good chuckle, looked a touch concerned. Her ears were flattened slightly. “Tobin, dear,” she whispered, barely louder than a sigh of wind through the trees, “the audience seems to be enjoying the labels more than the story. They are laughing at the words on the paper, not the words from the script.”

The labels were so sensible. Oh, so sensible and neat.

Tobin wriggled his nose, a sure sign he was thinking very hard. He knew what he had to do. It was the most daring thing he had ever considered. He had to change his labels. But the play was still going on. The actors were about to perform the grand finale, where the Princess declares her love for the gardener and they plant a seed together, a moment meant to be tender and hopeful.

He knew he had to trade his beloved perfect labels for a muddled, imperfect play. He pictured his neatest label, King’s Shiny Crown, peeling away from the crown. It felt like giving up a piece of his own heart. He felt the rough bark of the cardboard tree against his fur, heard the hushed intake of breath from the audience, and smelled the faint sweet scent of the prop roses as he dashed past. He took a deep breath that smelled of pine needles and damp earth. The Pot for Plants label needed to go on the seed, and the seed label needed to go on the pot. And the Watering Thingy needed to be a watering can again, plain and simple.

He dashed out from behind the cardboard tree, a tiny whirlwind of fur and fierce determination. He scurried onto the stage, his spectacles askew, almost tumbling into the middle of the performance. The audience gasped. Tobin, with a surprising burst of speed, snatched the label from the flowerpot. He then carefully plucked the tiny seed from its small paper bag, the one meant to symbolise hope and growth. With nimble paws he stuck the Pot for Plants label right onto the seed. Then he grabbed the empty flowerpot and stuck the label that was originally meant for the seed — Tiny Beginning of Future Greenery — onto the pot. He spotted the Watering Thingy and quickly peeled off its long complicated label, replacing it with a simple, hastily written Watering Can.

With a final triumphant wiggle of his stubby tail, he scurried back behind the curtain, his heart pounding, just as Iris was meant to pick up the seed.

Iris looked down. Instead of her Pot for Plants, she saw a tiny seed with a label that read Pot for Plants. She looked at it, a flicker of confusion in her bright eyes, then her eyes twinkled with understanding. She giggled, a sound that made Tobin’s heart swell, and picked it up. Then she looked at the flowerpot, now labelled Tiny Beginning of Future Greenery, and a wide smile spread across her face. She took the watering can and gave the pot a gentle watering, as if tending to a precious new life.

The audience, who had seen Tobin’s frantic scramble, erupted. They did not know why it was funny, but they knew it was. They understood the joyful unexpected turn. Iris and the Prince, now following their proper script, declared their love. They planted the seed now labelled Pot for Plants in the flowerpot now labelled Tiny Beginning of Future Greenery.

The forest itself seemed to sigh with relief, a gentle rustle of leaves that sounded like applause. The play was saved, not by perfect props, but by a bit of clever thinking and a lot of brave running.

As the final curtain of dandelion fluff drew closed, the applause was thunderous. It boomed and echoed through the trees, a joyous sound that made the ground tremble slightly. The villagers cheered for Iris, for Bartholomew, and especially for the brave little mole who had managed to turn a muddle into a masterpiece of mirth. They had never seen anything quite like it.

Tobin, his spectacles firmly back in place, felt a warmth spread through him, a feeling much nicer than even the neatest label. Backstage, the ladybug slept in her velvet pouch, unbothered by names. And as the stars began to pepper the velvet sky, Tobin knew the trees would remember a play that had wobbled and still stood up.
characters: Tobin (spectacled stagehand mole), Iris (marshmallow-fur princess rabbit), Aunt June (rustling-leaf director)
